summary: Provides IANA considerations for the ISO/IEC Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID), which some IETF protocols use. It describes how values are managed in the registry and is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: This is a rulebook for handing out numbers on a list that labels which kind of network message follows, so the IETF and IANA can keep it tidy.

questions: how does iana allocate nlpid values
subtitle: How IANA hands out the one-byte network layer protocol identifiers that ISO/IEC defined and some IETF protocols use.

tldr.problem: Some IETF protocols use the one-octet ISO/IEC Network Layer Protocol Identifier, but only a few code points are open to IANA, and the IETF had no rules for allocating them.
tldr.mechanism: New values are allocated by IANA under the IETF Review policy while code points last, the IEEE SNAP code point 0x80 is RECOMMENDED instead of a new one-octet value, and the ISO/IEC body that maintains the list is told of every allocation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC allocates 0xC0 to TRILL and 0xC1 to IEEE 802.1aq and records which code points in the 0xC0 range remain available.

today: RFC 6328 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 164) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why NLPID Rules Are Needed
sections.content:
Some protocols developed or extended by the IETF use the ISO/IEC Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID). The registry of NLPID values is maintained by ISO/IEC by updating ISO/IEC TR 9577. That document actually speaks of one-octet Initial Protocol Identifiers and Subsequent Protocol Identifiers; most values work as both, so this RFC calls them all NLPIDs.

ISO/IEC lets a code point be allocated without its approval, as long as the code point is not in a range categorized for another organization and ISO/IEC JTC1 SC6 is informed. This RFC specifies what level of IETF approval is needed to allocate a code point for IETF use, what IANA does, and related guidelines. RFC 5226 is incorporated except where this document says otherwise.
sections.eli5: A worldwide standards group keeps a list of one-byte labels for kinds of network messages. This RFC says how the IETF may add to that list without stepping on anyone's toes.

sections.title: Where NLPIDs Are Used
sections.content:
NLPIDs appear in several protocols. The RFC names the protocol type field of the multicast address resolution server protocol (RFC 2022), the same field in the NBMA next hop resolution protocol (RFC 2332), and the IS-IS Protocols Supported TLV (RFC 1195).

Appendix B lists further RFCs issued before the end of March 2009 that reference the NLPID, including RFC 1661 on PPP, RFC 2427 on Frame Relay and RFC 2684 on ATM adaptation layer 5.
sections.eli5: Several different network systems already use these one-byte labels to say what kind of message comes next, like a label on the front of a parcel.

sections.title: Sub-Ranges of the Code Space
sections.content:
ISO/IEC TR 9577 divides the 256 possible values into sub-ranges categorized for organizations, mainly ISO/IEC and the ITU-T. Examples are 0x00 for ISO/IEC, 0x01-0x0F for ITU-T, and 0x10-0x3F for ITU-T Rec. X.25 and ISO/IEC 8208. The value 0xFF is reserved for an extension mechanism to be developed jointly by ITU-T and ISO/IEC.

Only 0xC0-0xCF is listed as potentially available for IANA. All other ranges belong to other organizations.
sections.eli5: The list of 256 labels is split into blocks, and each block belongs to a different group. Only one small block was left over for IANA.

sections.title: The SNAP Code Point 0x80
sections.content:
NLPID 0x80 is the IEEE SNAP (SubNetwork Access Protocol) code point. It is followed by five octets, using the IEEE SNAP SAP conventions of RFC 5342, to specify the protocol. A valid five-octet sequence can start with the IANA OUI followed by two octets assigned by IANA.

The same IANA registry is used whether such an identifier is introduced by the 0x80 NLPID or by the IEEE SNAP SAP value 0xAAAA. Because few one-octet code points are available, using the SNAP NLPID is RECOMMENDED over allocating a new one-octet NLPID.
sections.eli5: One special label says that a longer label follows. Using that long label is better than using up one of the few short labels that remain.

sections.title: Code Points Still Available
sections.content:
Since few code points can be allocated by IANA, the RFC says it is desirable to use 0x80 where practical, or to get code points allocated from ranges categorized to other organizations. For example, 0x8E was allocated for IPv6 (RFC 2460) even though it lies in an ISO/IEC range. One-byte code points are assigned to TRILL and IEEE 802.1aq because they are meant for the IS-IS Protocols Supported TLV.

The table shows the state of the 0xC0-0xCF range after the two allocations made by this RFC: 0xC0 to TRILL (RFC 6325) and 0xC1 to IEEE 802.1aq. 0xCC is IPv4 and 0xCF is PPP.
sections.eli5: Only a handful of free labels are left in that block, so the rules say to look for other options first.

sections.title: What IANA Does
sections.content:
While code points remain, IANA allocates additional values when needed using the IETF Review policy from RFC 5226. Each time it allocates an NLPID, IANA informs the IETF liaison to ISO/IEC JTC1 SC6, or the IAB if it cannot determine the liaison. The liaison or IAB makes sure SC6 hears of it so ISO/IEC TR 9577 can be updated. The RFC says it is desirable that the IAB maintain such a liaison.

This RFC allocates 0xC0 and 0xC1, and IANA is to ask the liaison or the IAB to inform SC6. IANA also keeps a web page of NLPIDs allocated to IETF protocols or otherwise of interest. Appendix A gives its initial contents, such as 0x81 for ISO CLNP, 0x82 for ISO ES-IS and 0x83 for IS-IS.
sections.eli5: When IANA hands out a label, it must tell the standards group that owns the main list so everyone's lists stay the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it is concerned with the allocation of NLPIDs and is not directly concerned with security. It adds no security requirements of its own.
sections.eli5: This RFC is about handing out labels, not about keeping secrets, so it has nothing to add on safety.
